subtopics.title: Transactions, ACID Properties & Serializability
subtopics.subtitle: Transaction states, ACID, anomalies, schedules, precedence graphs and isolation levels

concepts.text: What a Transaction Is

A transaction is a logical unit of database work: a sequence of read and write operations that must be executed as a whole, such as transferring money between two accounts. It begins with BEGIN (or implicitly with the first statement) and ends with COMMIT, which makes its changes permanent, or ROLLBACK (ABORT), which undoes them. The DBMS treats the transaction as indivisible even though it is made of many low-level steps.
A transaction moves through five states (state diagram in words):
items: Active: the initial state; the transaction is executing its reads and writes.
Partially committed: the final statement has executed, but the changes may still be only in main-memory buffers.
Committed: the commit record has reached stable storage; the changes are permanent. Path: active -> partially committed -> committed.
Failed: normal execution can no longer proceed (logic error, constraint violation, system failure). Reached from active or partially committed.

Aborted: the transaction has been rolled back and the database restored to its state before it started; the system may then restart it or kill it. Path: failed -> aborted. Committed and aborted are both terminated states.

concepts.text: ACID Properties

rows: Bank transfer of Rs 500 from A to B
All operations happen or none do
If the system crashes after A is debited but before B is credited, the debit is undone
A correct transaction takes the database from one valid state to another
A + B is the same before and after the transfer; no balance goes negative
Concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate results
Another transaction summing A + B never sees A debited but B not yet credited
Once the user is told the transfer succeeded, a power cut cannot lose it
Recovery manager (redo using the log, stable storage)

concepts.text: Concurrent Executions and Anomalies

Running transactions concurrently improves throughput and resource utilisation, because while one transaction waits for disk I/O another can use the CPU. It also reduces average response time, since short transactions need not wait behind long ones. The price is that uncontrolled interleaving can produce anomalies, so the DBMS must restrict interleavings to those that are equivalent to some serial order.

rows: Two transactions read the same item and both write it; one write overwrites the other
T1 and T2 both read A = 100, T1 writes 150, T2 writes 80; T1's update is lost
A transaction reads a value written by another transaction that has not committed
T2 reads A written by T1, then T1 aborts; T2 used a value that never existed
A transaction reads the same item twice and gets different values
T1 reads A = 100, T2 updates A to 200 and commits, T1 reads A = 200
A repeated query with the same condition returns a different set of rows
T1 counts rows WHERE dept = 'IT', T2 inserts a new IT employee, T1 counts again

concepts.text: Schedules and Conflict Serializability

A schedule is the chronological order in which operations of several transactions are executed, preserving the order within each transaction. A serial schedule runs one transaction completely before the next starts and is always correct; a non-serial (interleaved) schedule is correct only if it is serializable, i.e. equivalent to some serial schedule. Two operations conflict if they belong to different transactions, access the same data item, and at least one of them is a write (read-write, write-read, write-write). A schedule is conflict serializable if it can be turned into a serial schedule by swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations.

concepts.plainText: Number of serial schedules of n transactions = n!

concepts.text:
Schedule S:  r1(A)  w1(A)  r2(A)  w2(A)  r2(B)  w2(B)  r1(B)  w1(B)
Conflicting pairs (earlier -> later):
  w1(A) ... r2(A)   gives edge T1 -> T2
  w1(A) ... w2(A)   gives edge T1 -> T2
  w2(B) ... r1(B)   gives edge T2 -> T1
  r2(B) ... w1(B)   gives edge T2 -> T1
Precedence graph: T1 -> T2 and T2 -> T1  => cycle
Result: S is NOT conflict serializable.
If r1(B) w1(B) came before r2(B), only T1 -> T2 exists:
acyclic, equivalent serial order T1, T2.
Precedence (serializability) graph test:
items: Draw one node per transaction.
For each conflicting pair where Ti's operation comes before Tj's, add a directed edge Ti -> Tj.
The schedule is conflict serializable if and only if the graph has no cycle; a topological sort of the graph gives an equivalent serial order.

concepts.text: View serializability is a weaker condition: a schedule is view equivalent to a serial schedule if every transaction reads the same initial values, reads each value from the same writer, and the same transaction performs the final write of each item. Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable, but not vice versa; the extra view-serializable schedules always contain blind writes (writes without a prior read). Testing view serializability is NP-complete, so practical systems enforce conflict serializability.
Recoverability of schedules (important when transactions abort):
items: Recoverable schedule: if Tj reads a value written by Ti, then Ti commits before Tj commits. Otherwise a committed Tj might depend on an aborted Ti, which cannot be fixed.
Cascading rollback: one abort forces several dependent transactions (that read its dirty data) to roll back too.
Cascadeless schedule: a transaction reads only values written by already-committed transactions, so no cascading rollback can occur. Every cascadeless schedule is recoverable.
Strict schedule: no transaction reads or overwrites an item until the last writer of that item has committed or aborted; produced by strict 2PL.

formulas.plainText: Number of serial schedules of n transactions = n!
Total schedules of k transactions with n1..nk operations = (n1 + ... + nk)! / (n1! n2! ... nk!)
Conflict serializable if and only if the precedence graph has no cycle

notes.text: To test a schedule, list only the conflicting pairs (same item, different transactions, at least one write) and draw edges in time order. Read-read pairs never create edges.
Conflict serializable is a subset of view serializable, which is a subset of all correct schedules. A view-serializable but not conflict-serializable schedule must contain a blind write.
Recoverable does not mean cascadeless. A schedule where Tj reads Ti's uncommitted write but commits after Ti is recoverable, yet aborting Ti still forces Tj to roll back.

formulas.title: Serial schedules
formulas.plainText: Number of serial schedules of n transactions = n!
formulas.description: Each ordering of the n transactions, run one after another, is a distinct serial schedule.

formulas.title: Total possible schedules
formulas.description: Counts all interleavings that keep each transaction's own operations in order; e.g. two transactions of 2 operations each give 4!/(2!2!) = 6.

formulas.title: Conflict serializability test
formulas.plainText: Conflict serializable iff precedence graph has no cycle
formulas.description: Add an edge Ti -> Tj for every conflicting pair where Ti acts first; any cycle means the schedule is not conflict serializable.

flashcards.back: Active, partially committed, committed, failed and aborted; committed and aborted are the terminal states.

flashcards.front: When do two operations in a schedule conflict?
flashcards.back: When they belong to different transactions, access the same data item, and at least one of them is a write.
One in which every transaction reads only data written by already-committed transactions, so an abort never forces other transactions to roll back.

flashcards.front: Which SQL isolation level prevents dirty and unrepeatable reads but still allows phantoms?

questions.questionText: For the schedule r1(X), r2(X), w1(X), w2(X), the precedence graph contains:
options: Only the edge T1 -> T2, so the schedule is conflict serializable
Only the edge T2 -> T1, so the schedule is conflict serializable
Edges T1 -> T2 and T2 -> T1, so the schedule is not conflict serializable
No edges, because read operations never conflict
questions.explanation: r1(X) before w2(X) and w1(X) before w2(X) give T1 -> T2, while r2(X) before w1(X) gives T2 -> T1. The cycle means the schedule is not conflict serializable (it is the classic lost-update pattern).

questions.questionText: Which SQL isolation level prevents dirty reads but still permits unrepeatable reads?
questions.explanation: Read Committed allows reading only committed data, so dirty reads are impossible, but another transaction may commit a change between two reads of the same item.

subtopics.title: Lock-Based Protocols & Deadlock Handling
subtopics.subtitle: S/X locks, two-phase locking, timestamps, wait-for graphs, wait-die and wound-wait

concepts.text: Shared and Exclusive Locks

A lock is a variable attached to a data item that controls how transactions may access it. A shared lock (S, lock-S) lets the holder read the item only, and many transactions may hold S locks on the same item together. An exclusive lock (X, lock-X) lets the holder read and write the item, and no other transaction may hold any lock on it at the same time. A transaction requests the lock from the concurrency-control manager and waits if the request is incompatible with locks already granted.
Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
Under 2PL each transaction issues lock and unlock requests in two phases:
items: Growing phase: the transaction may acquire locks but may not release any.
Shrinking phase: the transaction may release locks but may not acquire any new one.
Lock point: the moment the transaction obtains its final lock; ordering transactions by lock point gives an equivalent serial order.
Guarantee: every schedule allowed by 2PL is conflict serializable.
Limitations: basic 2PL does not prevent deadlock and does not prevent cascading rollback.

rows: Hold all exclusive (X) locks until commit or abort
Strict, cascadeless schedules; no cascading rollback
Hold all locks (S and X) until commit or abort
Transactions serialize in commit order; simplest to reason about
Acquire every needed lock before starting
Deadlock-free, but needs the lock set in advance

concepts.text:
T1 under strict 2PL (transfer 50 from A to B):
  lock-X(A)
  read(A); A := A - 50; write(A)
  lock-X(B)             <- lock point (last lock acquired)
  read(B); B := B + 50; write(B)
  commit
  unlock(A); unlock(B)  <- shrinking phase after commit

Lock conversion lets a transaction change the mode of a lock it already holds. An upgrade converts S to X and is allowed only in the growing phase; a downgrade converts X to S and is allowed only in the shrinking phase. Conversion improves concurrency because a transaction can read an item under a shared lock and take the exclusive lock only when it actually needs to write.

Timestamp ordering is a lock-free alternative: each transaction gets a unique timestamp TS(Ti) when it starts, and each item keeps its largest read timestamp R-TS(X) and write timestamp W-TS(X). An operation that would violate timestamp order (for example Ti writing X when TS(Ti) < R-TS(X)) causes Ti to be rolled back and restarted with a new timestamp. The protocol guarantees conflict serializability and is deadlock-free because no transaction ever waits, though it may cause starvation and cascading rollbacks; Thomas' write rule ignores obsolete writes.
Deadlock in Databases

A deadlock exists when every transaction in a set waits for a lock held by another transaction in the same set, so none can proceed. For example, T1 holds X(A) and requests X(B) while T2 holds X(B) and requests X(A). It requires the four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Deadlock is handled by prevention (never let it happen), or by detection and recovery (let it happen, find it, break it).

Wait-for graph (edge Ti -> Tj: Ti waits for a lock held by Tj)
  T1 waits for T2 (item B)   T1 -> T2
  T2 waits for T3 (item C)   T2 -> T3
  T3 waits for T1 (item A)   T3 -> T1
  T4 waits for T2 (item B)   T4 -> T2
Cycle T1 -> T2 -> T3 -> T1  => T1, T2, T3 are deadlocked.
T4 is not in the cycle: it is blocked, but not deadlocked.
Roll back one cycle member (e.g. T3) to break the deadlock.

concepts.plainText: Deadlock exists if and only if the wait-for graph has a cycle

rows: Scheme (Ti requests an item held by Tj)
Ti dies (rolls back, restarts with same timestamp)

concepts.text: Other prevention approaches deny one Coffman condition:
items: Lock all items at once before starting (conservative 2PL) removes hold and wait.
Impose a total order on data items and lock them only in that order (resource ordering) removes circular wait.
Preemption through wait-die or wound-wait; restarted transactions keep their original timestamp, so they eventually become the oldest and cannot starve.

concepts.text: Detection, recovery, timeouts and starvation:
items: Detection: the system maintains the wait-for graph and periodically searches it for cycles; a cycle means deadlock.
Victim selection: roll back the transaction with the least cost, judged by work done so far, locks held, work remaining and how many transactions would be involved.
Rollback: total rollback aborts and restarts the victim; partial rollback undoes it only as far as needed to release the required lock.
Timeout: a transaction that waits longer than a set interval is assumed deadlocked and rolled back; simple, but it may abort transactions that were not deadlocked.
Starvation: the same transaction repeatedly chosen as victim, or repeatedly overtaken in lock queues; avoided by counting rollbacks in the cost factor and granting locks in FIFO order.

formulas.latex: \text{Wait-die: } TS(T_i) < TS(T_j) \Rightarrow T_i \text{ waits, else } T_i \text{ dies}
formulas.plainText: Wait-die: if TS(Ti) < TS(Tj) then Ti waits, else Ti is rolled back

formulas.latex: \text{Wound-wait: } TS(T_i) < TS(T_j) \Rightarrow T_j \text{ rolled back, else } T_i \text{ waits}
formulas.plainText: Wound-wait: if TS(Ti) < TS(Tj) then Tj is rolled back, else Ti waits
Deadlock exists if and only if the wait-for graph has a cycle

notes.text: In both wait-die and wound-wait the older transaction is never rolled back. Remember: wait-die, the older one waits; wound-wait, the older one wounds.
Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability but NOT freedom from deadlock or cascading rollback. Strict 2PL removes cascading rollback; only conservative 2PL removes deadlock.
A transaction blocked behind a deadlocked set (like T4 in the example) is not itself part of the deadlock; only the transactions on the cycle are.

formulas.title: Wait-die rule
formulas.latex: \text{Wait-die: } TS(T_i) < TS(T_j) \Rightarrow T_i \text{ waits, else } T_i \text{ dies}
formulas.plainText: Wait-die: if TS(Ti) < TS(Tj) then Ti waits, else Ti is rolled back
formulas.description: Non-preemptive: an older requester waits, a younger requester is rolled back and restarted with its original timestamp.

formulas.title: Wound-wait rule
formulas.latex: \text{Wound-wait: } TS(T_i) < TS(T_j) \Rightarrow T_j \text{ rolled back, else } T_i \text{ waits}
formulas.plainText: Wound-wait: if TS(Ti) < TS(Tj) then Tj is rolled back, else Ti waits
formulas.description: Preemptive: an older requester forces the younger lock holder to roll back, a younger requester waits.

formulas.title: Deadlock detection
formulas.plainText: Deadlock iff the wait-for graph has a cycle
formulas.description: With single-instance locks, a cycle in the wait-for graph is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock.

flashcards.front: What are the two phases of two-phase locking?
flashcards.back: Growing phase, in which locks are acquired but none released, then shrinking phase, in which locks are released but none acquired.

flashcards.front: How does strict 2PL differ from rigorous 2PL?
flashcards.back: Strict 2PL holds only exclusive locks until commit or abort; rigorous 2PL holds all locks, shared and exclusive, until commit or abort.

flashcards.front: In a wait-for graph, what does an edge Ti -> Tj mean?
flashcards.back: Transaction Ti is waiting for a lock that Tj currently holds.

flashcards.front: Why do wait-die and wound-wait not cause starvation?
flashcards.back: A rolled-back transaction restarts with its original timestamp, so it eventually becomes the oldest and is never rolled back again.

questions.questionText: Transaction T1 holds a shared lock on item Q. Which request by another transaction T2 can be granted immediately?
options: An upgrade of T1's lock to exclusive on behalf of T2
No lock on Q until T1 commits
questions.explanation: Shared locks are compatible with each other, so T2 can also read Q. An exclusive lock is incompatible with any existing lock and must wait.

questions.questionText: Under the wait-die scheme, T5 with timestamp 5 requests an item held by T9 with timestamp 9. What happens?
questions.explanation: T5 has the smaller timestamp, so it is older. In wait-die an older requester waits; only a younger requester dies.

questions.questionText: Which modification of two-phase locking avoids cascading rollbacks?
options: Releasing shared locks as soon as the item is read
Allowing lock upgrades in the shrinking phase
Holding all exclusive locks until the transaction commits or aborts
questions.explanation: This is strict 2PL: no other transaction can read an item written by an uncommitted transaction, so an abort never cascades.

questions.questionText: A wait-for graph has edges T1 -> T2, T2 -> T3, T3 -> T1 and T4 -> T2. Which transactions are deadlocked?
options: None, because T4 breaks the cycle
questions.explanation: The cycle T1 -> T2 -> T3 -> T1 contains T1, T2 and T3. T4 waits for T2 and is blocked, but it is not on the cycle, so it is not part of the deadlock.

subtopics.title: Failure Classification & Log-Based Recovery
subtopics.subtitle: Failure types, stable storage, log records, WAL, undo/redo, checkpoints and shadow paging

concepts.text: Failure Classification

rows: Logical error (bad input, constraint violation) or system error (deadlock victim)
Power failure, OS or DBMS bug, hardware fault
Main memory (buffers) contents; disk intact (fail-stop assumption)
Redo committed, undo uncommitted transactions from the log
Head crash, media corruption during transfer
Part or all of the disk
Restore from backup/archive copy, then redo from the archived log

concepts.text: Storage types, by how well they survive failures:
items: Volatile storage: main memory and cache; fast, but contents are lost in a system crash.
Non-volatile storage: magnetic disk, SSD, tape; survives crashes but can still fail (disk failure).

Stable storage: an abstraction of storage that never loses data, approximated by keeping multiple copies on independent non-volatile media (for example RAID or remote replicas) and writing them one after another. The log must be kept on stable storage.

concepts.text: Recovery and Atomicity

A transaction may modify several data items, and a crash can happen after some of those modifications have reached disk but not others. To keep atomicity, the DBMS first writes information describing the modifications to stable storage, without modifying the database itself. After a crash this information lets the system undo the effects of transactions that did not commit and redo the effects of those that did, preserving both atomicity and durability. The most widely used structure for this is the log.
Log records (the log is a sequential file of records):
items: <Ti start>: transaction Ti has started.
<Ti, X, V1, V2>: Ti wrote item X, changing it from old value V1 to new value V2. The old value is used for undo, the new value for redo.
<Ti commit>: Ti has committed; once this record is on stable storage the transaction is durable.
<Ti abort>: Ti has aborted and its rollback is complete.

concepts.text: Write-ahead logging (WAL) requires that a log record for an update reach stable storage before the corresponding data page is written to disk, and that all log records of a transaction, including <Ti commit>, be forced out before the transaction is declared committed. This guarantees that whenever a modified page is on disk, the old value needed to undo it can be found in the log.
Deferred vs Immediate Modification

rows: Only after the transaction partially commits
While the transaction is still active
Redo only; no undo is ever needed

concepts.text:
Immediate-modification log at the moment of a crash:
  <T0 start>
  <T0, A, 1000, 950>
  <T0, B, 2000, 2050>
  <T0 commit>
  <T1 start>
  <T1, C, 700, 600>
  --- crash ---
Recovery: T0 has start and commit  -> redo(T0): A = 950, B = 2050
          T1 has start, no commit  -> undo(T1): C = 700, log <T1 abort>
Undo scans backward; redo scans forward. Both are idempotent.

concepts.plainText: Redo Ti if the log contains both <Ti start> and <Ti commit>

concepts.text: Checkpoints

Without checkpoints the recovery manager would have to scan the whole log and would redo many transactions whose updates already reached disk. A checkpoint writes all log records in memory to stable storage, flushes all modified buffer blocks to disk, and then writes a <checkpoint L> record listing the transactions L active at that moment. At recovery the system scans back only to the last checkpoint: transactions that committed before it need no action, transactions that committed after it are redone, and transactions in L or started after it with no commit are undone.
Other recovery techniques:
items: Shadow paging: the database keeps two page tables, a current table updated by the transaction and a shadow table that is never changed during it. Modified pages are written to new locations; commit simply makes the current table the new shadow by atomically updating a single on-disk pointer. No undo or redo log is needed, but it causes data fragmentation, needs garbage collection and handles concurrency poorly.
ARIES: the industrial log-based algorithm using log sequence numbers (LSNs), WAL and three passes (analysis, redo, undo) that repeats history and supports fuzzy checkpoints.

formulas.plainText: Redo Ti if the log contains both <Ti start> and <Ti commit>

formulas.latex: \text{undo}(T_i) \text{ if } \langle T_i\ \text{start}\rangle \text{ in log but no commit or abort}
formulas.plainText: Undo Ti if the log contains <Ti start> but neither <Ti commit> nor <Ti abort>

formulas.latex: \text{Scan range} = \text{log records from last checkpoint (and its list } L\text{) to end}
formulas.plainText: Recovery scans only from the last checkpoint (and transactions in its list L) to the end of the log

notes.text: Undo uses the OLD value and proceeds backward through the log; redo uses the NEW value and proceeds forward. Deferred modification never needs undo.
A system crash destroys volatile storage only; data on disk is assumed intact (fail-stop). Disk failure is the case that needs an archival backup.
A transaction that committed before the last checkpoint needs neither redo nor undo, because the checkpoint already flushed its updates to disk.

formulas.title: Redo rule
formulas.plainText: Redo Ti if the log contains both <Ti start> and <Ti commit>
formulas.description: A committed transaction's updates are reapplied using the new values so that its effects are durable.

formulas.title: Undo rule
formulas.latex: \text{undo}(T_i) \text{ if } \langle T_i\ \text{start}\rangle \text{ in log but no commit or abort}
formulas.plainText: Undo Ti if the log has <Ti start> but no <Ti commit> or <Ti abort>
formulas.description: An incomplete transaction is rolled back by restoring old values, scanning the log backward.

formulas.title: Checkpoint scan range
formulas.latex: \text{Scan range} = \text{log records from last checkpoint (and its list } L\text{) to end}
formulas.plainText: Recovery scans from the last checkpoint (and its active list L) to the end of the log
formulas.description: Checkpoints bound recovery work, since earlier committed transactions are already on disk.

flashcards.front: What does the log record <Ti, X, V1, V2> store?
flashcards.back: That Ti wrote item X, changing it from old value V1 (used for undo) to new value V2 (used for redo).

flashcards.front: Why does deferred modification never need undo?
flashcards.back: The database is written only after the transaction partially commits, so an incomplete transaction has changed nothing on disk.

flashcards.front: What three steps does a checkpoint perform?
flashcards.back: Flush all log records in memory to stable storage, flush all modified buffer blocks to disk, then write a <checkpoint L> record to stable storage.

flashcards.front: How does shadow paging commit a transaction?
flashcards.back: By atomically switching the single on-disk pointer from the shadow page table to the current page table.

questions.questionText: With immediate modification, the log at a crash is: <T1 start>, <T1, A, 500, 400>, <T1 commit>, <T2 start>, <T2, B, 300, 350>. After recovery, what are A and B?
questions.explanation: T1 has start and commit, so it is redone and A = 400. T2 has no commit, so it is undone using the old value and B = 300.

questions.questionText: In log-based recovery with deferred database modification, which operation is required after a system crash?
options: Neither; the database is always consistent
questions.explanation: Writes reach the database only after partial commit, so uncommitted transactions changed nothing and need no undo; committed ones may need redo.

questions.questionText: T1 commits before the last checkpoint, T2 commits after it, and T3 is active at the crash. Which action does recovery take?
options: Undo T1, redo T2, ignore T3
Ignore T1, redo T2, undo T3
Redo T1, undo T2 and T3
questions.explanation: The checkpoint already flushed T1's updates, T2 committed after the checkpoint so it is redone, and T3 never committed so it is undone.
